newsitem.title: USA: Ben & Jerry's founder sued in nut dispute.
newsitem.headline: Ben & Jerry's founder sued in nut dispute.

text.p: For the environmental activist with a sweet tooth, each pint of Ben & Jerry's Rainforest Crunch ice cream promised help for the Amazon.

But despite the best intentions, Community Products Inc., the company that Ben & Jerry's Homemade Inc. formed to make that ice cream has been unprofitable for years and is now the subject of a nasty lawsuit.

It seemed like a good idea back in 1989 when Cohen met an activist at a Grateful Dead concert who suggested the Vermont ice cream maker use Amazon nuts harvested on a sustainable basis, giving Amazonians an alternative to logging.
"I wanted to start a company where the social mission would be supreme, that would be the whole purpose of the company and that profit was a means to that end," Cohen said in an interview.

CPI started well, helping establish the first nutshelling cooperative in the Amazon. Its mandate was to donate 60 percent of its profits to non-profit groups, and it made enough money to donate $550,000 in the early 1990s to conservation and peace organizations.
CPI produced a peanut brittle snack called Rainforest Crunch, but its biggest customer was Ben & Jerry's, which used Brazil nuts in its Rainforest Crunch ice cream and Rainforest Crunch Peace Pops.
Each pint of the ice cream said that the purchase of the nuts helped the "Brazilian forest people start a nut-shelling cooperative."

However, the former production manager at CPI, who was fired in December 1994 after five years with the company, is suing the company and Cohen, charging that he was dismissed because he refused to "cover-up" company problems.

Irv Deutsch alleged in court papers that the Brazil nuts shipped to CPI were contaminated with coliform, the company may have violated tax laws, and that plans to install equipment at CPI's Montpelier, Vt. plant would create "workplace safety issues."

In addition, the lawsuit, filed in Washington Superior Court in Montpelier, alleged that the only nuts used in the Ben & Jerry's ice cream came from commercial sources and not from the Brazilian cooperative run by the Xapuri Indians.
Deutsch's lawyer, Scott Cameron, said Deutsch was promised permanent employment, but was fired when an investigative reporter began asking questions about CPI.

"We have a suspicion that there was a connection," he told Reuters. "They didn't act like socially-reponsible, progressive, liberal whatever they are. They acted like the worst kind of self-serving capitalists from old days."

In 1995, Ben & Jerry's was criticized for its earnest message on Rainforest Cruch ice cream and the amount of Brazil nuts it used from a most unlikely source -- the ice cream maker's own 1994 annual report.
Only about 5 percent of the nuts in each pint of the ice cream actually came from the co-ops, the rest from commercial suppliers, the company's "social auditor" said in the report.

Cohen said CPI was buying all the nuts the co-operative could produce, and was forced to buy from commercial sources to make up the difference. Ben & Jerry's soon changed the label to refocus on the rainforest rather than the Indians.
Now, CPI sources from two nut cooperatives based in Peru and Bolivia, which supply 85 percent to 100 percent of the Brazil nuts in each pint of Ben & Jerry's Rainforest Crunch.
"No matter how you buy your nuts, whether form a commercial processor or a coop, all have been grown wild in the rainforest and gathered by rainforest people," Cohen said.

He said Deutsch's charges are false. Coliform bacteria is present on almost everything and usually harmless, he said. Ben & Jerry's tests for coliform in all its finished products and no one has ever gotten sick. CPI also has had no problems with state or federal tax authorities, Cohen said.

Mark Sherman, who has headed CPI for the last two years, said the company has bought equipment which cut physical labor, and has developed a proprietary process to cleanse microbiological bacteria often found in nuts.
Cohen said Deutsch levelled the charges just to money. "He's definitely looking for cash," he said.
As for CPI, Cohen said it has raised demand for Brazil nuts and supported cooperatives in the Amazon and raised environmental awareness in Amazon.
"It's hard to call an unprofitable business a success," he said. "In terms of its mission, which was to increase demand for Brazil nuts, it certainly did that."
